name: cracked broken asphalt road crumbling into dirt, laid as a road network with crossroads and dead ends
label: wasteland_ruins/asphalt

answer.evidence: The image is a flat, top-down tileable ground texture 176 px wide and 192 rows tall, with a full-width silhouette. It shows brown dirt with grey-blue asphalt road strips forming crossroads, T-junctions and dead ends. The roads have only a thin dark shadow along their south edges. They show no vertical front face and no raised top surface, so the picture is a flat map view. That is expected for a terrain tile, but it has no 3/4 structure.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 7 visible tones per 16x16 tile, equal to the paving reference and well above the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so no large flat fills. The dirt carries speckle grain, hairline cracks and small pale pebbles. The asphalt patches have mottled, per-pixel dithering in several slate tones, plus a darker slate rim that blends into the neighbouring material. It is not a uniform black sticker line, and the 0% neutral share of dark edge pixels backs that up. There are about 4-5 lightness steps on both the dirt and the asphalt, close to the reference ramps. The palette is small (14 colours in total) but yields the same visible richness as the references. The weak points are that the asphalt blobs have fairly blocky silhouettes, and the dirt texture is somewhat uniform noise rather than clustered. Neither is enough to look thinner or flatter than the references.

surfaces.part: ground tile with asphalt road network on dirt

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain tile seen from straight above. It is a full 176x192 opaque field of dirt with grey-blue asphalt road segments (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends, an isolated block and a patch). The roads have no raised front face and no top/front split. Only a thin dark 1-row shadow sits under the lower edges of the road shapes, which reads as an outline and not a vertical face. The silhouette is a uniform 176-wide rectangle on every row. The ground-plane texture is appropriate for terrain, so the kind matches.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts put the candidate at 7 visible tones per tile, which matches the paving reference (7) and beats the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, so no 5x5 areas are flat. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines lean brown or blue-grey rather than black. By eye, the asphalt patches have darker rims in the material's own tone and no uniform black sticker line. The dirt ground carries speckle grain, small pebbles and hairline cracks, and the asphalt has mottled blue-grey variation. The ramps run about 4-5 steps per material against roughly 6 on the paving reference. Only 14 colours are used in total, but the locked palette explains that, and the visible texture is not much thinner than the reference. The crack lines are sparse and the asphalt interiors are fairly uniform, so texture is 'some' rather than 'rich'. The piece holds up beside the references without looking flat or sticker-like.

There is no standing volume, no front face, no eave line and no ellipse. The dark shadow pixels along the south edges of the road patches are only a thin edge outline. The kind is terrain, so this flat top-down view matches the intended use, though it has no 3/4 structure.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 7 visible tones per 16x16 tile, equal to the paving reference (7) and above the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no flat fills. The column scans show only texture changes between dirt (#7b5d48, #8d8482) and asphalt (#516268, #3d4b51), with no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical south face. The dark pixels along the road bottoms are small edge shadows on a flat surface, not a front face. For a terrain tile this is the expected top-down appearance, but it has no front face of 3 or more rows.
